report:
**Conclusion: no—not on current evidence.** Whole-body vibration (WBV) has *not* been shown to prevent osteoporotic fractures, so it should not be considered a fracture-prevention treatment in place of proven osteoporosis care.

The best direct evidence is a systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials in adults aged ≥50. It evaluated fractures as well as falls and bone measures, but the available trials were limited and did not establish a statistically reliable reduction in fractures. Any possible benefit appears more plausibly related to balance, muscle function, or fewer falls than to a demonstrated reduction in fragility fractures. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6027066/

Importantly, a review focused on women with osteoporosis concluded that research on WBV’s **direct effect on fracture reduction is sparse**. It suggested WBV *might* improve fracture-risk factors (e.g., aspects of balance/neuromuscular function), but called for more studies—not evidence that it prevents fractures. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6372741/

Some studies and meta-analyses report modest improvements or less decline in bone-mineral density (BMD), particularly in postmenopausal women. But BMD is a surrogate outcome: it does not by itself prove fewer fractures, and vibration protocols, duration, and participants vary substantially. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y

For a person with osteoporosis, WBV may be an optional, supervised adjunct to safe exercise if clinically appropriate, but it should not replace fracture-risk assessment, medications when indicated, adequate calcium/vitamin D, and established fall-prevention/strength-and-balance exercise. Current guidance emphasizes fall prevention alongside pharmacologic therapy and conventional exercise. https://www.aafp.org/afp/2023/0700/practice-guidelines-osteoporosis-treatment
